lesson.text: Quick memory: in grade 6 you read closely. What is an inference? (A conclusion you reach from clues in the text and what you already know.) Today: choose the evidence that proves your point best.
When you make a claim about a text, back it with evidence: a short quote, or a close paraphrase. But not all evidence is equal. Some proves your claim, some only hints at it, and some proves nothing.
The strongest evidence is relevant, about your claim; specific, the exact words, not a vague summary; and hard to read any other way. Weak evidence could prove something else too.

Read: “Kofi checked the knot three times before he let the boat drift out.” Claim: Kofi is careful. The words “checked the knot three times” prove it best. “He let the boat drift out” says nothing about care.

Some claims are explicit: the text says them in so many words. Others are inferences, read between the lines. For an inference, pick the detail that points to it most clearly. What a character does can outweigh what they say.

Read: “Sam shrugged and said the test didn't matter. Then he read his notes on the bus, at lunch and in the queue.” Claim: Sam wants to do well. His words say no, but his actions say yes: they are the stronger evidence.
Several pieces of evidence can build a case, but one precise quote beats three loose ones. Keep quotes short, then explain the link: point, evidence, explain. Evidence never speaks for itself.
Try it in the world: when a friend says a story's hero is brave, ask which exact words prove it best. Then try it on a book you are reading. Next: dialogue and incidents.

exercises.prompt: Read: “Lena's voice shook as she read out her poem, and she gripped the paper with both hands.” Claim: Lena is nervous. Which words prove it best?
exercises.hint: Which words show a feeling, rather than just what happened?
exercises.explain: “Lena's voice shook” shows her nerves directly; reading a poem out or holding paper could happen with any feeling.

exercises.prompt: A vague summary is stronger evidence than a text's exact words.
exercises.hint: Which is easier to check against the text?
exercises.explain: False: exact words are specific and can be checked; a vague summary may hide what the text really says.

exercises.prompt: Claim: the storm was frightening. Sort the evidence.
items: “even the dog hid under the bed”
exercises.hint: Does each quote show fear or danger?
exercises.explain: Banging shutters and a hiding dog show how frightening the storm was; the paint and the day of the week say nothing about it.

exercises.prompt: Read: “Mo yawned, rubbed his eyes and sat down heavily.” Which of these is an inference, not explicit?
exercises.hint: Which one did you have to work out from clues?
exercises.explain: “Mo yawned” and “Mo sat down” are in the text; that he is tired is worked out from those clues.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.hint: Two words are about arguing, and two are about how a text says things.
exercises.explain: A claim is what you argue; evidence backs it up; an inference is worked out from clues; explicit means said in so many words.

exercises.prompt: Read: “It was a warm spring. By June the wells ran dry and the cattle had to be moved away.” Claim: the drought was severe. Which words prove it best?
exercises.hint: Which words show how bad things became?
exercises.explain: Dry wells show the drought was severe; a warm spring and a month name prove nothing about how bad it was.

exercises.prompt: Claim: Jo loves music. Order the evidence from the weakest to the strongest.
items: “Jo practises piano every morning before school”
exercises.hint: Which shows the most time, effort and feeling for music?
exercises.explain: Owning a radio proves little; humming shows some interest; practising every morning before school shows real love for music.

exercises.prompt: Claim: Tom is generous. Which evidence is strongest?
choices: “Tom gave his last sandwich to a friend”
exercises.hint: Do actions or words prove more? And which one costs Tom something?
exercises.explain: Giving away his last sandwich costs him something, so it proves generosity best; saying he likes sharing is weaker.

exercises.prompt: Read: “At noon the baker hung up a sign saying closed, then wiped her eyes.” Sort the statements.
exercises.hint: Find each one in the text's own words; if you had to work it out, it is inferred.
exercises.explain: The sign and the time are in the text. That she is upset, and that something sad has happened, come from the clue of her wiping her eyes.

exercises.prompt: One precise quote can be stronger than three loose ones.
exercises.hint: Is evidence about how much you give, or how well it proves the point?
exercises.explain: True: one exact, relevant quote proves a point better than several that only hint at it.

exercises.prompt: Claim: Nia is kind. Evidence: “she gives up her seat on the bus”. Which sentence explains it best?
choices: It shows kindness: she puts others first.
exercises.hint: Explaining says how the evidence proves the point.
exercises.explain: “It shows kindness: she puts others first” links the action to the claim; the others do not explain anything.

exercises.prompt: Read: “Grandma never said she missed Grandpa. But every evening she set out two cups.” Claim: Grandma misses Grandpa. Which words prove it best?
choices: “every evening she set out two cups”
exercises.hint: What she does may say more than what she says.
exercises.explain: Setting out two cups every evening shows she still thinks of him; what she says points the other way, so her actions are the stronger evidence.

exercises.prompt: Put the paragraph in order: point, evidence, explain.
items: Checking three times shows he takes no risks.
Kofi is careful with the boat.
exercises.hint: Start with what you claim, then prove it, then explain how.
exercises.explain: First the point: Kofi is careful. Then the evidence: he “checked the knot three times”. Then the explanation: checking three times shows he takes no risks, so the quote proves the point.

exercises.prompt: Claim: the town was proud of its new bridge. Sort the evidence.
items: “its picture went on the town's flag”
exercises.hint: Which quotes show a feeling about the bridge, and which only describe things?
exercises.explain: Cheering crowds, the flag and “the town's jewel” show pride. Steel, rain and a wide river are facts that prove nothing about pride.

exercises.prompt: To prove an inference about a character, what they do can be stronger evidence than what they say.
exercises.hint: People sometimes say one thing and do another.
exercises.explain: True: actions often show true feelings. When words and actions disagree, as when Ana says she does not care but polishes her trainers, the actions usually prove more.

exercises.prompt: Claim: the narrator feels left out. Which quote is strongest?
exercises.hint: Which quote is directly about being left out?
exercises.explain: “Nobody saved me a seat” shows the narrator was not included. A noisy hall could go with any feeling, and sitting down shows no feeling at all, so both are weak.
